name: Missing Balancing Loop
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Thermostat That Was Never Installed
lesson.summary: Healthy systems pair every strong reinforcing loop with a balancing loop capable of restraining it, and the central systems-thinking diagnosis behind quantum computing skepticism is that the hype reinforcement loop currently lacks a balancing loop strong enough to keep public and financial claims tethered to physical reality.
lesson.body:
The balancing feedback loop chapter made a general claim about systems: a reinforcing loop running without any balancing loop attached to it does not simply grow, it eventually grows until something breaks it, either an external limit it slams into or a collapse when the story it has been amplifying turns out not to match reality. Systems that sustain healthy long-run behavior almost always have a balancing loop paired with their reinforcing loops, some mechanism that measures the gap between claim and reality and pulls the system back when that gap grows too large. The missing balancing loop is the diagnosis that the hype reinforcement loop described earlier in this section does not currently have an adequately strong partner of that kind.

It helps to ask what a healthy balancing loop for quantum computing claims would actually look like. It would need to play the thermostat's role: a way to measure the gap between what is being claimed publicly and what has actually been demonstrated, and a mechanism that reliably translates a large gap into corrective action, retracted claims, adjusted funding, tempered coverage. Peer review is a candidate, but it operates slowly relative to the news cycle and mainly filters what gets published, not what gets amplified afterward. Failed replications and critical technical papers exist, but they routinely receive a small fraction of the press coverage given to the original announcement, since a correction is a less exciting story than a breakthrough. Most funders and journalists lack the expertise to independently evaluate a disputed claim, so the scrutiny that would need to happen fast enough to matter often does not.

A recurring pattern illustrates the asymmetry well. When a lab announces a quantum advantage or supremacy result, a demonstration that a quantum device did something believed to be intractable for classical computers, that announcement typically generates broad press coverage within days. When classical computer scientists subsequently find a smarter classical algorithm that closes much or all of the claimed gap, as has happened more than once in this field's history, that follow up work tends to circulate mainly within specialist circles and rarely reaches the audience that heard the original claim. The correction is real, but it is structurally quieter than the claim it corrects, which is exactly the signature of a balancing loop that is present but too weak to do its job.

Calling the loop missing is a simplification worth immediately qualifying: it is not that zero corrective mechanism exists, it is that the mechanism is underweighted relative to the reinforcing loop it is meant to restrain. The named skeptics covered in the remaining chapters, Gil Kalai, Michel Dyakonov, Leonid Levin, are best understood as exactly this kind of underweighted balancing mechanism: technically serious critiques that circulate and get debated within expert communities, then largely fail to reach the scale of attention given to the claims they respond to.

The useful move is to treat the balancing loop being missing or weak not as a complaint but as a diagnosis you can act on, precisely the mindset the next chapter, on leverage points, is built around. If a system is unstable because a balancing loop is too weak, the fix is not necessarily to slow the reinforcing loop directly, often difficult and politically costly, but to identify where a stronger balancing loop could be installed, a question with a surprisingly well developed answer in the systems thinking literature.
